subject: (EXTERNAL) Indiana Ave homeless shelter comment
comment: Victoria, Thank you for taking the time to talk with me today about a few Westside issues. Would you please enter my comment to the City Council representatives who will be addressing the new homeless shelter on City property today? Thank you. Regards, Adam Gmyrek I, Adam Gmyrek, would like to go on record; I am against the new homeless shelter disguised as the "tiny home village" being built on the Salt Lake City property at 1850 W Indiana Ave, Salt Lake City, UT. The new "tiny home village" model is a disguise for a homeless shelter; the people who will be living at the tiny home village are being removed from local homeless shelters and placed into a new form of shelter for the homeless — are they not? It is my understanding that the residents who will be awarded to live at the 413-acre parcel owned by the City of Salt Lake are currently homeless and reside at one of the several homeless shelters within Salt Lake City — is this not a true statement of fact? Name it what you want, call it what you choose, Palmer Court, Freedom Landing, Sunrise Metro, Magnolia, Wendell etc., it is a homeless shelter, plain and simple. The people who will be living there are being removed from the local homeless shelters. The goal of the tiny home village is to house people who are homeless; is it not? Thus, a homeless shelter. The Westside does not need another homeless shelter to enhance its community; the Westside has already been enhanced and burdened with the fast tracking of 2 homeless shelters that were created within the last 3-years. Has your memory faded? Finally, entering into a 40-year contract with The Other Side Academy is fiscally irresponsible. The contract with The Other Side Academy should be between 3 to 5 years and then reviewed with attaining its set goals at year 2 or 4 years. If the City then deems The Other Side Academy fit to operate the modern day homeless shelter then a longer contract should be granted. I am emphatically against this modern day homeless shelter. Adam Gmyrek

subject: The Other Side Village Vote
comment: I believe wholeheartedly that The Other Side Village is good for the community as well as the individuals who will live and be impacted there. Not only am I confident in the leadership team, I am confident in the people they work with and the transformative/uplifting nature of how they go about their mission. I've had the pleasure of interacting with leadership, employees, interns, and many of the graduates/members of The Other Side Academy -- they've proven their ability to turn lives around. Support, community, accountability, and other aspects of their programs/operations restore and strengthen the dignity, integrity, and health of those who experience homelessness or have committed crimes. Their work -- and my interactions with them and their graduates -- inspired me while I was a student and continues to influence both how I approach my career and how I view and interact with people that are frequently misjudged and misunderstood. In decisions like these, far too often the influential voices are those who have great wealth, those who desire to maintain property value, or those with little respect for others who look or act differently than the college grad standard of success. Please know there are so many of us who have been silent — we hope for this to be approved, we are ready to support the mission and vision, we believe it will be the kind of help and success that deep down we all yearn to live for. While dozens may be opposed, fearful, or upset — hundreds are in favor and hoping we will do the right thing in approving and supporting this cause. And, I believe, thousands will be positively impacted by living there and by affiliation. If not here, where? If not now, when? If not us, who? (Just imagine that being read by some cool coach in a touching football movie or something haha). "...when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you something to drink? When did we see you a stranger and invite you in, or needing clothes and clothe you? When did we see you sick or in prison and go to visit you?" The King will reply, 'Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me and I can do better. Let's do better now.

subject: "The Other Side Village"
comment: Dear City Council, I'm writing to urge you to vote in favor of building The Other Side Village. There have been many comments made from concerned neighbors about how this village will affect crime rates in the neighborhood. It's fair that these people are correlating homelessness with an increase in crime; people in desperate situations will take drastic actions that others can't even imagine. However, I'd like to point out that with the construction of The Other Side Village, we will not simply be concentrating homelessness in this one neighborhood. The difference here is that these people will no longer be homeless. The Other Side Village will not only offer these people a safe place to sleep, eat and shower, but it will also offer a community with a social network of support. These people who were once in a desperate situation will finally have their basic needs met and will be able to be contributing members of society. The Other Side Village concept is not simply "another place to put homeless people"; it's a solution to homelessness. Please remember this as you listen to comments from people who don't want a homeless camp in their backyard. No one wants a homeless camp in their backyard. The Other Side Village WILL NOT be a homeless camp. It will be a community of engaged citizens. It will be our first step in ensuring that we do not have homeless camps built in any more backyards. Thank you! Emma Scanlon

subject: Budget amendment No. 3 from Sept 20, 2022
comment: To City Council, Concerning Budget Amendment No. 3: A one-time $6 million amount to address what you're calling "deeply affordable" housing is not going to actually solve the problem we have. I hope that is understood and I hope no one upon the council is under such a false pretense. This amount of money will not go nearly far enough to actually address and change the issue of homelessness and recurring homelessness in Salt Lake City. The definition of what is considered "affordable" is what needs to be addressed and changed as soon as possible. Currently, it being at 80% AMI is frankly ridiculous, considering the AMI is usually shown to be at least 60k, sometimes exceeding 70k. This is such a load of b.s. because you're taking the exceptionally wealthy people and grouping them in with folks that are making hardly anything, and pretending there is actually some sort of middle ground they can meet in (the median). To truly meet the needs in terms of affordability in rent, you must reduce what is considered "affordable" in your definitions and policies from 80% down to 30%. The council and this year's budget, the way it is written, is incentivizing landlords and developers, both predatory professions by nature, for essentially not doing anything, except accepting slightly less money for owning property. There is nothing in the incentive program that demands that landlords/developers must make necessary improvements to properties, nor is there anything about required maintenance. And there should be! It is shameful on them, and the City Council, for not doing more to address inequities in this City, especially when some have so much, and many have so little. Please do take and use the $6 million, but get back to public meetings, public hearings, and discuss how you will get "affordability" on track to reflect what is actually affordable for most people in need, and not just make it about any given area's "median income". Or if you're going to keep it that way, using median income, define "affordable" as 30% AMI instead of 80% AMI. Thank you. -James Miska

subject: The Other Side Village
comment: Dear City Council, The summer before I moved to Salt Lake City, my friends and I were discussing my upcoming move across the country. "Did you know they actually solved homelessness in Salt Lake City?", one friend asked. "Yea, I heard about that. The actually use Housing First policies there," another friend agreed. I was ecstatic to move to a city that actually made big steps towards providing housing to our most vulnerable neighbors. Now 6 years later, I am reminded everyday how misled my friends were. I am reminded everyday that I live in a city that is too scared and too inert to do anything towards this problem. Where I live, when I look out my window, the people I usually see are transient folks hanging out on the park strip across the road from my house. A few years ago, during one cold stretch in the dead of winter, a young man lived under a pile of blankets and would wait for hours at a time at night, right outside my kitchen window. As a citizen of this city, this hard on me. I don't like living in a city where my neighbors' basic needs aren't being met. I want to live in the city my friends told me Salt Lake was. I am very excited to hear about The Other Side Village. I think this model is very aligned with the Housing First ideal I put a lot of hope in; the concept that led my friends to think that Salt Lake had solved homelessness. I think a community of modest, affordable housing and strong social supports is a great first step in undoing this mess of homelessness we have here in this city. I strongly believe that homelessness is not indicative of the flaws of the individuals affected but instead it is indicative of the flaws of the city that allows it. I ask you to vote in favor of buildingThe Other Side Village. Thank you.
